note: Our own writing about the real courses, keyed by the name on the card. Used in preference to GSPro's description, which for many courses is a sentence of club marketing or nothing at all. Facts here are about the real place, not the sim build.

descriptions.Whistling Straits: Pete Dye built this on two miles of Lake Michigan shoreline in 1998, on what had been a flat army airfield. Everything you see was moved there: the dunes, the fescue, and something close to a thousand bunkers, many of them small enough to be decorative and all of them, officially, in play. That detail cost Dustin Johnson the 2010 PGA Championship when he grounded his club in one on the last and never knew it was a bunker at all. Three PGA Championships and the 2021 Ryder Cup.
descriptions.TPC Scottsdale (Stadium): Weiskopf and Morrish, 1986, built in the desert north of Phoenix with spectators in mind before anyone else was doing it. The 16th is the result: a 160-yard par 3 enclosed on all sides by grandstands holding twenty thousand people who drink all day and boo anything short. Nowhere else in golf sounds like it. The rest is a fair, wide desert course that would be unremarkable without the week in February that makes it famous.
descriptions.Adare Manor: A Robert Trent Jones Sr course from the 1990s that J.P. McManus had Tom Fazio take apart and rebuild in 2016, down to every blade of grass. The result is immaculate rather than rugged, laid along the River Maigue in County Limerick with the manor house behind. It hosts the 2027 Ryder Cup, which is why the renovation happened. Parkland golf in a country better known for its links.
descriptions.Prestwick Golf Club (Tournament): The Open Championship started here in 1860 and stayed for the first twelve, which makes this the oldest championship venue in golf. Old Tom Morris laid it out over twelve holes on a strip of Ayrshire duneland. It still plays like something from before the rules settled down: blind drives over the Cardinal bunker at the third, the Himalayas at the fifth played entirely over a dune with nothing to aim at, and a closing stretch that modern design would never permit. Not a test of golf so much as a reminder of where it came from.
descriptions.Cypress Point: Alister MacKenzie's 1928 course on the Monterey Peninsula, and the one architects name when asked for the best. It runs through pine, then dune, then out onto the rocks: the fifteenth and sixteenth sit on the Pacific, the sixteenth a 230-yard par 3 played across an inlet of open ocean with no bail-out worth the name. Barely more than two hundred members. Most people will only ever see it in a simulator.
descriptions.Pacific Dunes: Tom Doak, 2001, the second course at Bandon and the one that made his name. It breaks the rules cheerfully — back-to-back par 3s on the back nine, four of them in total, an out-and-back routing that ignores the usual nine-and-nine — and gets away with it because every hole sits where the ground wanted one. Several run along the cliff edge a hundred feet above the Pacific. Walking only, like everything at Bandon.
descriptions.Teeth of the Dog: Pete Dye spent three years living on site in the Dominican Republic before this opened in 1971, and seven of its holes run directly along the Caribbean with the water in play on every one. Dye's own line was that he created eleven holes and God created seven. Still the best course in the Caribbean by common consent, and the one that turned Casa de Campo into a resort worth flying to.
descriptions.Fishers Island Club: Seth Raynor's last course, finished in 1926 on an island off the Connecticut coast that you reach by ferry or not at all. It is a catalogue of the template holes Raynor and C.B. Macdonald borrowed from Britain — Redan, Biarritz, Punchbowl — laid across a peninsula with Long Island Sound on three sides. A tiny membership and a short season keep it unknown to most golfers and ranked in the world's top ten by everyone who has seen it.
descriptions.Ohoopee Match Club: Gil Hanse, 2018, built in the sandhills of south Georgia for one purpose: match play. There are no stroke-play tees in the usual sense and the card is close to irrelevant — you choose a line, your opponent chooses theirs, and the holes are wide enough that both can be right. Fast, firm, sandy ground that plays the way the Carolinas sandhills used to before irrigation. A private club with no tournament ambitions at all.
descriptions.Payne's Valley: Tiger Woods's first public-access design, opened in 2020 in the Missouri Ozarks at Big Cedar Lodge. Wide fairways and big greens by intent — it was built for resort golfers, not to defend par. The thing everyone remembers is the extra hole afterwards: a par 3 played down into a limestone sinkhole with a waterfall behind the green, designed by Johnny Morris rather than Woods, and not counted on the card.
descriptions.Tiburon (Great White / Hammerhead): Greg Norman's Naples course, laid out through cypress and pine with coquina shell waste areas instead of rough — you can ground your club, but you cannot predict the lie. It hosts the QBE Shootout each December and the LPGA's season finale. Flat Florida ground made interesting by sand rather than by earth-moving.
descriptions.Lew Wentz Memorial: A Perry Maxwell municipal in Ponca City, Oklahoma, from the 1930s, paid for by an oil man who gave most of his money away. Maxwell's greens are the reason it is worth knowing: the same restless contouring he brought to Prairie Dunes and to Augusta's back nine, on a course anyone could afford to play. One of the best public courses in the state and almost unknown outside it.
descriptions.Royal County Down: Newcastle, County Down, with the Mountains of Mourne behind the clubhouse and the Irish Sea down one side. Old Tom Morris was paid four pounds for the original layout in 1889. It is the most beautiful links in the world and one of the most unfair: blind tee shots over marram-topped dunes, bunkers with eyebrows of rough hanging over them, and gorse that takes a ball permanently. Rated first in the world more often than anywhere else.
descriptions.Pebble Beach: Jack Neville and Douglas Grant, 1919, laid out by two amateurs who routed it along the cliffs of Carmel Bay and left the interior holes to fend for themselves. The stretch from the sixth to the tenth sits directly above the Pacific, and the seventh — barely a hundred yards downhill to a green on a rock — is the most photographed short hole in golf. Six US Opens. The only one of the world's great courses anyone can book by phone.
descriptions.Carnoustie: The hardest of the Open rota, and it does not look it: flat Angus farmland with no dunes to speak of and nothing picturesque about it. The difficulty is in the wind, the bunkering, and the Barry Burn, which crosses the eighteenth fairway twice and finished Jean van de Velde in 1999 when he stood in it with his trousers rolled up. The closing three holes are the hardest finish in championship golf.
